text: In October 2004, Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen stepped aside as chief executive. The family handed the company to someone outside the family for the first time. The young man from the strategy department. Jørgen Vig Knudstorp. He was thirty-five.
He had spent three years studying how LEGO made and lost money. His first goal was not growth. It was survival. Get cash under control, and cut what the company couldn't afford.

The family stayed on as owners, and backed him. Even when the cuts reached Legoland, the park the family had opened in Billund in 1968. In 2005, LEGO sold seventy percent of its four Legoland parks to the investment firm Blackstone, for three hundred seventy-five million euros.
Then the pieces. Designers were told to work with what already existed. The catalog of different elements was cut roughly in half, to about seven thousand.
With fewer pieces, the sets went back to what kids actually build: police stations, fire trucks, race cars.
LEGO went back to the big retailers that had called it unfocused and self-centered, and planned its year around what they needed.

And it started listening to fans it had mostly ignored: adults. Years earlier, in 1998, a student had cracked open LEGO's new robot brick and published how it worked. LEGO didn't sue. In 2005, the new chief executive went to a fan convention himself.
It worked faster than almost anyone expected. In 2005, LEGO was back in profit: about five hundred million kroner.
